h: Life on board, and how to plan your dive
p: Stand inside HMS Alliance for a few minutes and the numbers start to sink in. Dozens of men lived, worked and slept in that space for weeks on end, with bunks squeezed next to torpedoes and the smell of diesel everywhere. Guided tours on board, often led by people with a real feel for submarine life, bring out the little details you'd walk straight past otherwise, such as how crews kept clean, what they ate and how they coped with being cut off from the world.

Give yourselves at least a couple of hours. Alliance alone deserves a good chunk of time, and the galleries are worth a proper look rather than a quick skim. Families with younger children will find plenty to keep them interested, but it really comes alive for kids from about eight upwards who can follow the stories and cope with the ladders.

Wear flat, sensible shoes, because hatches, rungs and narrow walkways don't mix well with sandals. Anyone who struggles with tight spaces might want to dip in and out rather than tackle the whole boat in one go. And if you're coming over from Portsmouth, the Gosport Ferry is a quick and very easy way across the harbour.

The museum sits at Haslar, close to the mouth of the harbour, so step outside and you'll get views of ships coming and going. Combine it with the nearby Explosion Museum for a full naval day, or finish up with a breezy walk along the seafront at Stokes Bay.
